books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Civil Rights Act of March 1, 1875, Section 1, 18 Stat. 335
Civil Rights Cases, 109 U.S. 3 (1883), majority opinion of Justice Joseph P. Bradley

stimulus.text:
“That all persons within the jurisdiction of the United States shall be entitled to the full and equal enjoyment of the accommodations, advantages, facilities, and privileges of inns, public conveyances on land or water, theaters, and other places of public amusement; subject only to the conditions and limitations established by law, and applicable alike to citizens of every race and color, regardless of any previous condition of servitude.”

—Civil Rights Act of 1875, Section 1 (March 1, 1875)
stimulus.source_note: Civil Rights Act of March 1, 1875, Section 1, 18 Stat. 335. Public domain (federal statute; text verified against Cornell LII, Civil Rights Cases, 109 U.S. 3 (1883)).

stem: The Civil Rights Act of 1875 was Congress’s last great Reconstruction law. The act most directly tried to

options.text: give Black men the vote in federal elections.

options.text: divide the South into military districts.
options.misconception: Background: the military districts came from the Reconstruction Acts of 1867.

provide land to freed families in the South.

rationales.A: Background: voting rights came from the Fifteenth Amendment; this act is about inns, trains, and theaters.
rationales.B: Background: the military districts came from the Reconstruction Acts of 1867.
rationales.C: The act names inns, trains, theaters, and other public places, and promises every person their full and equal enjoyment. It aimed at daily life, where a Black citizen could sleep, sit, and eat, not at the ballot box.
rationales.D: Background: Congress never passed a land-redistribution law; “forty acres” remained a broken promise.
rationales.general:
1. The act lists the places of daily life: inns, trains, theaters, and other public amusements.
2. It promises every person the full and equal enjoyment of those places.
3. The promise applies alike to citizens of every race and color.
4. So the act reaches past the ballot box into the ordinary day of a Black citizen.
Remember: a law’s list of places tells you exactly which part of life it was written to change.
